description: elodin, a filtering DNS forwarder. Everything here comes from the endpoint enabled by metrics.enabled; see the Metrics section of the README for what each series means.

panels.description: Queries accepted from clients, whatever became of them.
panels.title: Queries

panels.description: Share of queries answered from a sink list or a block rule.
panels.title: Blocked

panels.description: Cache hits as a share of cache lookups.
panels.title: Cache hits

panels.description: Share of queries that produced no answer. Amber past 1%, red past 5%.
panels.title: Failed

panels.description: Upstreams not currently in their failure cooldown.
panels.title: Upstreams up

panels.description: Time since the process finished starting up.
panels.title: Uptime

panels.description: From elodin_build_info. One value per instance.
panels.title: Version

panels.description: Composition of what happened to each query. These do not sum to the query rate: a query the backlog or the allow list turned away never reached an outcome, and one answered from a local zone is not counted apart. See the panels to the right.
panels.title: Answers by outcome

panels.description: Six different problems, kept apart on purpose. Rising drops means server.workers is too low; rising refusals means a client is not on server.allow_from; refused connections means max_connections is full or one client prefix has filled its share of it (the log line says which); rate-limited connections means a prefix is opening them faster than server.rate_limit.responses_per_second allows, which is arrival rather than occupancy and is the only series a handshake flood shows up on; failed connections means the OS would not start a thread, which happens below the limit and is not fixed by raising it. Accept backoffs are the odd one out: not connections at all, but seconds this server spent unable to accept any - a few while a burst clears and then steadily while it does not - about one a second per listener out of descriptors, about twenty for one meeting a stream of per-connection errors - so a flat line rather than a spike is a listener that has stopped taking connections entirely. When that is the cause this series goes flat rather than climbing - the metrics endpoint accepts through a loop of its own and cannot be scraped either, so the scrape gaps and up goes to 0. The msg=stats log line is the reading that survives it.
panels.title: Turned away, and not accepted

panels.description: Responses the limiter held back, and the fraction of those answered truncated instead so a real client retries over TCP.
panels.title: Rate limiting

panels.description: Answers that carried a valid chain of signatures, and answers refused because they did not. A step change in bogus is usually one zone.
panels.title: DNSSEC verdicts

panels.description: Rules in each set. A refresh that fetched a truncated list shows here as a drop, before anything shows up as a name that stopped being blocked.
panels.title: Filter rules loaded

panels.description: One series, so the title names it and no legend box is needed.
panels.title: Cache hit ratio

panels.description: Against cache.max_entries. A flat line at the ceiling with evictions rising means the cache is too small.
panels.title: Cache entries

panels.description: Against cache.max_bytes. An entry's size is decided by whoever answered the query, which is why this bound exists as well as the entry count.
panels.title: Cache size

panels.description: A miss costs an upstream round trip; a hit does not.
panels.title: Cache lookups

panels.description: Entries dropped to stay inside max_entries or max_bytes. Sustained evictions with a falling hit ratio is the signal to raise one of the two.
panels.title: Cache evictions

panels.description: By the name in the configuration. Under the race strategy every upstream is asked, so these sum to more than the forwarded rate.
panels.title: Queries per upstream

panels.description: The cumulative latency counter divided by the query counter beside it, so this is the mean round trip over the window rather than an average since start, which would stop moving.
panels.title: Mean upstream latency

panels.description: Exchanges that produced no usable answer. Three consecutive failures put an upstream in its cooldown, which shows in the panel beside this.
panels.title: Upstream failure rate

panels.description: 0 while an upstream is in its failure cooldown. Labelled as well as coloured, so the state never rests on hue.
panels.title: Upstream health

panels.description: User plus system CPU, in cores. 1.0 is one core saturated.
panels.title: CPU

panels.description: Virtual size is not plotted beside this: it runs three orders of magnitude larger and would flatten the line that matters. It is a stat below instead.
panels.title: Resident memory

panels.description: The descriptor limit is not plotted here: it is five orders of magnitude larger and would flatten both lines. It is the headroom stat below. Descriptors climbing while the connection count sits still is a leak rather than load.
panels.title: Threads and descriptors

panels.description: The one number that says whether this server is keeping up. Queries queue when every worker is inside an upstream round trip; a backlog that does not return to zero is server.workers set too low, and it turns into dropped queries once max_pending is reached.
panels.title: Worker pool backlog

panels.description: TCP, DoT and DoH connections each hold a thread. The dashed line is server.max_connections.
panels.title: Connections

panels.description: Address space reserved, which is mostly thread stacks and is not memory in use.
panels.title: Virtual memory

panels.description: When the process began serving. A change here is a restart.
panels.title: Started

panels.description: Open descriptors as a share of RLIMIT_NOFILE. The limit is usually far above anything server.max_connections implies, so this moving at all is worth a look.
panels.title: Descriptors in use
